title: Chapter 11: Lies, Damn Lies, and Backtests

claims.text: Crowding, chance, parameter selection and data-specific rules can all separate simulated returns from later experience.
Reject fake orders intended to mislead other participants; the author's anecdote is not an accepted execution practice.
Track-record dispersion can arise from random entries and selection, so a winning record alone does not establish superior skill.
claims.anchor: random effects play a large role

claims.text: Parameter sensitivity analysis is useful, but selecting a historical optimum does not guarantee improved future performance.
Discontinuous performance under small parameter changes is a warning to investigate dependence on particular trades and state transitions.
claims.anchor: Traders call this phenomenon a cliff

claims.text: Count instances of the specific rule and disclose the entire search, rather than presenting one favorable result among thousands as independent evidence.

assimilation: Keep a search ledger, distinguish selected historical results from untouched observations, inspect parameter neighborhoods and dependent samples, and account for liquidity and crowding without deceptive orders.
adversarial_review: The hypothetical stop-triggering profit is not guaranteed: orders can disappear, prices move adversely and fills fail. The unnamed system's decline is not causal proof of front-running. Random simulations require seeds, complete distributions and identical policies; the filtered random-entry example includes a trend filter with purported edge, so page 142's subsequent no-edge wording is misleading. The population of excellent traders and their probabilities are assumed, not measured; assessing personalities does not remove uncertainty. Regression toward the mean is a conditional statistical tendency, not a deterministic law of inherited traits. Optimization can overfit even with few parameters, and arbitrary unoptimized parameters need not provide unbiased estimates. The symmetric horizontal-shift story is an assumption; real surfaces may change shape. Page 150 reverses the effects of shifting a curve right/left at an ascending point. Figure 11-6 caption mentions moving-average days although its axis is drawdown threshold. The 41.4%/56% base result differs from the prior chapter's reported test, with no reconciliation. A risk reduction rule's rare activation is not itself proof it is useless; the demonstrated data-dependent selection and recovery trap are the issue. No particular sample count alone establishes statistical usefulness.
memory_delta: Do not infer skill or future returns from a selected track record. Audit all trials, parameter sensitivity, rule-specific sample counts and recovery behavior. Separate useful sensitivity analysis from claims that optimized peaks are predictively superior. Exclude deceptive order tactics.
reading_provenance: Read all PDF pages 136-156 and inspected figures 11-1 through 11-6, checking actual chart pages rather than caption-only pages.
